text:
The directness of a free kick relates to the severity of the infringement - direct free kicks are awarded for more severe issues  and may score a goal without touching any other player, while indirect free kicks are for less severe issues  and must touch another player before counting as a goal. It's fairly reasonable that the team being awarded the free kick would never have the extra burden of the free kick being considered direct against their own goal - the kick being direct serves to punish the defending team, and shouldn't put the offense at any risk at all. An indirect free kick certainly wouldn't count if kicked directly into either goal, and it would be odd if the offense was put at risk of an own-goal by their opponent committing a greater direct-kick infraction, when they wouldn't have been at any risk at all had the opponent committed a lesser indirect-kick infraction.

Effectively, a free kick is always considered indirect against your own goal. Other types of play restarts are similar - a throw-in is always indirect and cannot score without being touched by another player, whether it's in your own goal or not.

There are various attempts to develop such metrics; while nothing is standardized (as far as I know), the activity tracking app Strava has a feature called Grade Adjusted Pace (https://support.strava.com/en-us/articles/15402117-grade-adjusted-pace-gap):

Grade Adjusted Pace takes into account the steepness of terrain during your runs and estimates an equivalent pace on flat land. Because running uphill requires extra work, your Grade Adjusted Pace on ascents will be faster than your actual pace. Similarly, when running downhill, your Grade Adjusted Pace will tend to be slower than your actual pace.

The difference between GAP and actual pace generally becomes larger as the grade steepens. Athlete data has shown that the downhill adjustment peaks around -10%, after which it becomes slightly less extreme. Note that GAP does not account for the technical difficulty or condition of the terrain.

Law 12 (https://www.theifab.com/laws/latest/fouls-and-misconduct/#disciplinary-action) doesn't define a fixed threshold. The referee has to decide whether the player was attempting to deceive the referee. The cautionable offence is:

attempts to deceive the referee, e.g. by feigning injury or
pretending to have been fouled (simulation)

The amount of contact isn't the deciding factor. What matters is whether the referee believes the player is reacting to the challenge or trying to influence the decision. A player who dramatically exaggerates minor contact to sell a foul for a harsher sanction may also be guilty of attempting to deceive the referee. And of course the viewpoint of the referee matters. Just because we see it, doesn't mean the referee does.

That's why the threshold is usually much higher. A mistaken caution for simulation is difficult to undo, while simply waving play on rarely causes controversy. Unless the deception is obvious, many referees keep the card in their pocket. That's why Law 12 arguably allows more cautions for simulation than are actually shown... especially to players who are well known for their exaggeration.

text:
The simple answer is that however unlikely that is to be, two teams could theoretically end up with the exact same rating, down to two decimals places. You don't want to have to figure out a tie-breaker on the fly for what is arguably one of the most watched sports event on the world.

More realistically, I would hazard that this is at least initially surely a left-over from when FIFA first switched to the current ranking system in 2018. Ratings were initially rounded to the nearest integer; which could readily result in two teams having the exact same rating at a given point in time. This happens for ex. all the time in chess (where there are arguably many more rated competitors, but even looking at say the extreme end of the distribution, the top 100, will reveal several ties: see the FIDE rating list on their website (https://ratings.fide.com/top_lists.phtml?list=open)). Looking at the current FIFA ratings (as of July 11th 2026) also reveals a few teams which would in effect be tied if the numbers were rounded to the nearest integer; in fact even some teams which are separated by only 0.01 rating points:
 [image: FIFA rankings: 53. Costa Rica 1456.03; 54. Romania 1455.89; 55. Mali 1455.59; 56. Qatar 1450.31; 57. Iraq 1446.28; 58. Ireland 1441.10; 59. Slovenia 1441.09; https://i.sstatic.net/LWDP7Cdr.png]  (https://i.sstatic.net/LWDP7Cdr.png)

FIFA changed the rounding to two decimal places in April 2021, thereby greatly reducing the potential for ties of this kind, but not eliminating it. The first ratings published after this change in fact even included two pairs of teams tied with the same rating(!), see here (https://inside.fifa.com/fifa-world-ranking/men/news/italy-denmark-climb-as-qualifiers-make-their-mark). Unless the mentioned teams don't play any games, or only play draws against each other (resulting in no exchange of points), the mathematical coincidences required for this to persist over several rating periods are however vanishingly unlikely.

So, TLDR, it might be unlikely but it's not impossible.

The goal would have been legal if the ball went in.

Law 13 (https://www.theifab.com/laws/latest/free-kicks) covers free kicks. The only requirement on the kicking team is that the ball is stationary. There is no mention of the other team being ready. There are requirements on where the other team can be, but these do not restrict the kicking team. There is no need to wait for a whistle unless the referee has held up the game for safety, substitutions, discipline or some other reason.

IFAB provides this guidance (https://www.theifab.com/laws/latest/guidelines/body-language-communication-and-whistle/) on whether a whistle is needed for a restart.

The whistle is NOT needed to:

stop play for a clear:

goal kick, corner kick, throw-in or goal

restart play from:

most free kicks, and a goal kick, corner kick, throw-in or dropped ball

and

If the referee wants the player(s) to wait for the whistle before restarting play (e.g. when ensuring that defending players are 9.15m (10 yd) from the ball at a free kick) the referee must clearly inform the attacking player(s) to wait for the whistle.

That same page offers this FAQ that seems relevant.

[Question] Team A is awarded a direct free kick close to the opponents’ penalty area. The referee clearly informs the attacking player(s) to wait for the whistle before restarting play and approaches Team B players to ensure they respect the required distance from the ball. At the same time, Team A player takes a free kick before the referee gives a signal to do so. What is the correct decision?

[Answer] The free kick must be retaken and the player who took the kick is cautioned (yellow card) for unsporting behaviour.

If Messi took the kick quick too soon, the referee would have shown him the yellow card and required the kick be taken again. He did not. The implication is the kick was legal, and the goal would have stood.

text:
A referee's decisions are final, so unless you can show a misapplication of the LoTG, corruption, or some other serious integrity issue, the result stands. They are not immutable, but they are very hard to get overturned.

Law 5 (https://www.theifab.com/laws/latest/the-referee/#decisions-of-the-referee)

The decisions of the referee regarding facts connected with play,
including whether or not a goal is scored and the result of the match,
are final.

If the referee says they judged a situation as violent conduct, serious foul play, abusive language, whatever, the match result normally survives that. A bad factual decision is usually just that... bad, but final. The competition might later cancel a red card suspension, or punish the referee, but the result usually stays.

A wrong application of the LoTG is different. If the referee gets the rules themselves wrong, then the competition rules may allow a protest. For example, calling a penalty for a foul on the halfway line. But this depends on the competition's rules.

And if the issue is not just incompetence but actual bias, corruption, match-fixing, or deliberate manipulation, then it becomes a disciplinary matter. The referee could be suspended or banned, and the league authority may have powers to order a replay (depending on the competition rules).

So for your example of penalties and cards galore: whether the result is overturned would depend on whether this was merely terrible refereeing, a misapplication of the Laws, or something like proven corruption.
label: rulebook

In practice, FIFA have the ability to run the tournament as they see fit - while they can't force Canada to allow anyone entry, they could for instance rearrange the match so it is played in the United States. FIFA chose not to do so in the Partey case, but that doesn't mean they wouldn't in more extreme cases. Yes if you are an elite athlete; around 2008-9 there was a huge "technology war" in swimming which ended up with all elite athletes wearing full-body polyurethane suits due to the performance advantages they give. Most world records were broken in this time, often by considerable margins.

Restrictions have been introduced since then which mean that knee-length jammers are the maximum coverage allowed for men, and similarly knee-length suits which don't cover the shoulders or arms for women. These probably still give a performance advantage over traditional swimwear, but less so.

text:
The holes in a pickleball affect how air moves around (and through) the ball as it spins, which changes how the ball moves through the air. The size and number of those holes definitely has an impact, and the irregular position of the holes in a wiffle ball makes the movement more unpredictable (or predictable if you know how to align them).

Baseballs and golf balls have similar effects from the seams and dimples, but the effects are different by design. Golf balls have dimples to reduce drag, while the seams on a baseball create uneven air movement which changes the ball flight as it spins.

Wiffle ball holes are also horizontal, much longer than the holes of a pickleball. How does that affect the way it flies compared to a pickleball?

It changes the effect of those holes on the flight - spinning the ball in the direction of the "slots" has a different effect than spinning it perpendicular to the slots. This is one way wiffle ball pitchers can control the movement to some degree.

text:
The current distance is fixed by rule 2.01 (since 2023, see further below):

The grass lines and dimensions shown on the diagrams are those used in many fields, but they are not mandatory and each Club shall determine the size and shape of the grassed and bare areas of its playing field, except as follows:

(a) The grass line of the outer boundary of the infield dirt shall be a 95-foot radius from the center of the pitcher’s plate. A Club will be considered to be in compliance with this provision if the average distance of the grass line of the outer boundary of the infield dirt is less than 96 feet but more than 94 feet, and no individual measurement is more than 96 feet or less than 94 feet.

I however don't see a specific reason for the specific distance of 95 ft given there. The very first fields were very much improvised (this early game (https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/7e/First_known_photograph_of_a_baseball_game_in_progress.jpg) is taking place on what looks very much like a cricket pitch), nor does it appear in any previous rulebook. Since the later half of the 19th century only the dimensions between the bases, foul lines, base coaches' boxes &c had been defined, but there is not a single mention of the infield arc's distance - see this SABR article (https://sabr.org/journal/article/the-evolution-of-the-baseball-diamond-perfection-came-slowly/). Early fields in fact do not appear to have all necessarily have included such a line (the basepaths and the area behind homeplate in this 1879 picture (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Category:Black_and_white_photographs_of_baseball_teams#/media/File:1879_Providence_Grays.jpeg) are clearly the only bit of dirt on the infield) although the presence of an infield arc was obviously well established at some point by the start of the 20th century, as it is clearly visible in footage from then, see here (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fZord0btVkc)).

There's probably something to be said, in the early days at least, about the cost of maintaining grass given all the damaged possibly inflicted by the typical running/walking/sliding &c which are common place in baseball, but that again does not single out a specific distance. It serving as a useful delimitation and reference for umpires and players is more likely to at least be informed by tradition and typical play - infielders usually play some distance back from the basepaths to give them a fighting chance at covering ground balls which are not hit directly at them (the opposite strategy, playing the infield in to enable quicker and shorter throws, is usually only employed to prevent a runner on third from scoring).

For youth leagues (where the base-to-base distances are less than 90 ft) playing on purpose-built fields, the arc will typically be smaller: it is 50 ft from the pitcher's plate in the Little League World Series, for example.

So in short it appears there isn't an exact reason for why it is exactly (within tolerances) 95 ft, although you would have difficulty in defending much larger or much shorter measurements for this. Some things are just... well, traditional, in this case probably shaped by some amount of trial and error.

I'll note that since the 2023 rule change limiting the infield shift, the infield arc/grass line is not just a formality but actually the official limit of where the infield is, per rule 5.02(c)(i):

At the time the pitcher is on the rubber and begins the natural
movement associated with the delivery of the ball to the batter, the
defensive team must have a minimum of four players (in addition to the
pitcher and the catcher) with both feet completely in front of the
outer boundary of the infield dirt;

text:
You have already received a good answer regarding your example of the 100m dash. However, it should be noted that other sports may have other rules, and even in the 100m dash, rules have changed.

Let's first discuss alternative strategies for sprints in athletics: generally speaking, a race is aborted and re-set following a false start. However, what happens to the athlete who caused the false start differs between different regulations and at different times in history:

An athlete who causes a false start receives a warning, and is disqualified upon causing a false start for the second time.

If there is a false start, the entire field receives a warning, and if there is a second false start, the athlete(s) who caused it will be disqualified immediately, regardless of whether they were involved in the first false start or not.

An athlete who causes a false start is disqualified immediately.

A disqualified athlete may be allowed to still run "under protest".

An example that works closer to what you suggest is Formula 1: a car that moves before the start signal receives a 5 second time penalty. This is not exactly what you had in mind, because it does not simply nullify the advantage gained, which is usually only on the order of milliseconds. That time penalty needs to be served during a pit stop, where the pit crew is not allowed to touch the car for 5 seconds. If the car does not make a pit stop until the end of the race, the 5 seconds are added to the finishing time.

The toe-assisted ones (Lutz, flip, toe) make up half of those, so its not just just the placement of the pick. The Axel is the big exception. It takes off forward.

All of these are landed backwards. So, the skater entered most jumps and exits all jumps backwards. This leads to a significant amount of time skating backwards.

Speculation to address a comment: When the skater flexes their knees and leans prior to jumping, they shift their center of gravity ventrally. If they are skating forward, that could be unstable, especially if it's shifted ahead of their skates. Skating backwards, shifting the the center of gravity ventrally would be counterbalanced by the skater's backward momentum.

text:
This is common -- at all levels, high school, college, and NFL -- on punts. After the ball is punted, a few different things can commonly occur:

a player from the receiving team catches the ball (either "on the fly" or after a bounce) and attempts to advance. Players from the kicking team try to tackle the receiver.

a player from the receiving team makes a "fair catch" -- they catch the ball on the fly and make no attempt to advance. The play is dead at that point and the kicking team are not allowed to make contact with the receiver

no player from the receiving team tries to possess the ball. This is likely what you have seen: The ball will be "downed" at the point a member of the kicking team first touches the ball or if no one does, wherever the ball comes to rest*. Until the ball is downed or at complete rest, it would be legal for a receiving team member to grab the ball and attempt to advance, so it is common for members of the kicking team to surround the ball, especially if it is slowly rolling backwards (from the receiving team perspective). The kicking team is gaining a (slight) advantage in yardage and by surrounding the ball, making it highly unlikely that a receiving team member will risk trying to get the ball.

My (admittedly anecdotal) experience is that at the high school level it is much more common for no receiving member to attempt to catch the ball, while in the NFL one of the first two outcomes listed above is much more likely.

(*) There are a few details about exactly how and when a ball is "downed" on a kick, but this is the basic idea.

text:
The Football Video Support (VS) system is new review system primarily devised to help Football Associations / Competitions with fewer financial / human / technological resources, whereby they are unable to implement VAR, implement a decision review system.

Football Video Support (VS) is the answer to several requests that FIFA has received from those member associations that cannot implement the video-assistant-referee (VAR) system because their human and financial resources are limited and very few cameras are in use in their competitions.

What is Football Video Support? (https://inside.fifa.com/innovation/news/what-is-football-video-support)

For the FIFA youth tournaments - these are unlikely to be played in large stadia with VAR infrastructure in place, hence why VS is likely used, in addition to being trialed at a tournament.

VS is similar in its decision making approach whereby, if a review is called for, the referee goes to the Referee Review Area (RRA) to review the incident in question on a monitor. The evidence presented to the referee must be conclusive evidence of a mistake for the decision to be overturned.

The only real difference is that the review is instigated by one of the teams, and the game is stopped for the review; there is no "background checking" or "silent checks" made by the off-field official like there is in VAR.

Similarly to VAR reviews are limited to the following incidents:

The VS system is used only in the event of a possible clear and obvious error or serious missed incident in relation to the following scenarios:

a. Goal/no goal

b. Penalty/no penalty

c. Direct red cards (not second cautions)

d. Mistaken identity (when the referee cautions or sends off the wrong player of the offending team)

What is Football Video Support? (https://inside.fifa.com/innovation/news/what-is-football-video-support)

The reviews can only be requested by the team's Head Coach (or whoever the senior team official is on the sideline), and the request must be made immediately after the referees decision has been made.

The Head Coach must make a "finger twirl" hand signal to the Fourth Official, and hand over their team's Review Request Card. The Fourth Official will then signal to the Referee that a review has been submitted, and as soon as applicable the game is stopped for the review.

Only the team’s head coach (or, in their absence, the senior team official present in the technical area) can make a review request, which must be made immediately after the incident, by twirling their finger in the air and giving a review request card to the fourth official.

[...]

The fourth official will inform the referee of the review request and, if play has stopped (and not restarted) since the incident, the referee will go to the referee review area (RRA) to review the replay footage.

What is Football Video Support? (https://inside.fifa.com/innovation/news/what-is-football-video-support)

During the current trial phase, each team is allowed to make two (2) requests per match - however if their review is successful, and the referee's on-field decision is overturned, they get to keep that review. This is similar to other review/challenge systems seen in Cricket, NFL, Tennis for example.

During the IFAB's 139th Annual General Meeting, the decision was made to allow trials of the VS system to take place in non-FIFA competitions, opening the way for Football Associations to implement shortlisted solutions in their own tournaments.

Following the decision at The International Football Association Board’s 139th Annual General Meeting, FVS trials have been extended to non-FIFA competitions.

text:
There are a few possibilities I can think of that I would consider in this situation in order to get into a position to play the black - none are particularly easy...

Play the shot with running side (right-hand spin), and maybe a touch of top-spin, aiming the object ball to the far jaw of the pocket; that is, the right-hand side of the pocket. The object of this is to canon the cue ball into the black ball, running it off the bottom rail and off the side rail moving it into a more favourable position and opening up multiple pockets.

Play the shot straight, with screw and a little check-side (left-hand spin). The object here is to screw the cue ball of the side rail, and with the check-side the cue ball will move further up the table, leaving a more manageable angle on the black ball into the same pocket as the striped ball.

Play the shot to hit the object ball into the rail just before the pocket, and play with screw. Because of the pockets on American pool tables being angled (rather than rounded on English pool tables), the pockets are quite forgiving as to the accuracy needed, as such you can hit the object ball into the rail first, and it still goes in. Doing so will open up the angle of the screw giving it a similar effect to number 2 above.

Experience and ability would probably be the main factor in choosing which approach to go for:

Option 1 is probably the most difficult as it would require a bit of finesse and touch to judge the amount of spin to apply to get the required canon, and you're relying on a little bit of luck with the canon.

Option 2 would require a decent amount of power as well as good cueing - adding side spin with the additional power would push the cue ball off-line, meaning greater sighting/aiming is required.

Option 3 is probably the easiest of the three, but still requires good cueing.

According to Baseball-Reference, after 6 games in the 2013 season John Buck had a BA of .400 and OBP of .391 (https://www.baseball-reference.com/players/gl.fcgi?id=buckjo01&t=b&year=2013).  I assume that's what's being referred to here

In those 6 games he had 23 plate appearances, of which 8 were hits, 12 were non-productive outs, 1 was a walk, and 2 were sacrifice flies.  He had 8 + 12 = 20 total at-bats, so his BA was 8/20 = 0.400.   He had (BB + HBP)/(BB + HBP + SF) = (1 + 0)/(1 + 0 + 2) = 1/3 = 0.333.  His OBP was therefore 9/23 = 0.391.

When (BB + HBP)/(BB + HBP + SF) < H/AB then you get OBP < BA - in this case we have that, with 1/3 < 8/20.   But this is rare, because walks are much more common then sac flies.   For example in the 2013 season as a whole there were in MLB 14640 walks, 1536 HBP, and 1219 SF, so (BB + HBP)/(BB + HBP + SF) = 0.930!  It will only happen with small samples, early in the season.

text:
In simple English: blocking is when the ball goes from the opponent, I (we) jump and prevent/try to prevent it from entering our side. The ball can miss our hands, it can go through the block to our side, can go "out", it can rebounce to the opponent's arms, or anywhere else - it is still a block. Also I can block with my head (I dream) if it is higher than the net. And the ball can touch many blockers: it is still one collective block.

now:

FIVB rules

from the official FIVB rules 14.1.1, 14.1.2, 14.1.3:

Blocking is the action of players (1) close to the net (2) to intercept (3) the ball coming from the opponent (4) by reaching higher than the top of the net, regardless of the height of the ball contact

A block attempt is the action of blocking (5) without touching the ball.

A block is completed whenever (6) the ball is touched by a blocker.

(1), (2), ..., (6) - are mine

more details

(1) close to the net there is no exact definition of "close to the net" - sometimes it could be 1m, and the "Beach Volleyball Casebook" even says "it can depend of how tall the blocker is", because a taller blocker can jump farther from the net and his arms are still pretty close to the net. So it's the referee's decision, but usually it is obvious.

(2) to  intercept - there is another question about "intercept by spiking", I think people will add the oficial ruling for curious cases to that question: sports/q/16103 (https://sports.stackexchange.com/q/16103/13140)

(3) from the opponent - the ball must come from the opponent, and it is not a block when a player "imitates the block action" after a set.

(4) higher than the top of the net - what is often missed here: a blocker must have something (arm, finger, nose) higher than the top of the net. So, if my pinky is higher than the net - I can save the ball with my foot and it is still a block.

(5) blocking without touching - libero can not even TRY to block (14.6.6). So in a weird case when a back-row player of TeamA attacks from the first line higher than the net (which is forbidden), and a TeamB libero attempts to block (any part of the body higher than the net) - it is libero's fault, because the attacker's error occurs AFTER libero's error (attack is completed when the ball completely crosses the net/is touched by an opponent -- FIVB 13.1.3). Weird case, but obviously: the action can be a block, even without a contact with the ball.

(6) the ball is touched by a blocker - this definition allows back-row player to "attempt to block", and if the ball didn't touch ANY blocker ("ANY" is important) - then the block is not "completed", and thus - legal.

Also, one can "block the block" - if the ball rebounced from opponent's block and the player is intercepting it back - then it is a "block of another block"

text:
You want to get what makes a prediction "good" versus just "close"?

Since there's no single official, standardized metric for this, the best wayis to build a layered scoring system.

A Scoring System for Tennis

We can organize the scoring into three levels: from the big picture down to the fine details.

Example Scenario:

Actual Result: Federer defeats Nadal: 4-6, 6-3, 6-2.

Your Prediction: Federer to win: 7-5, 6-4.

NOTE: Left number is for Federer.

Level 1: The Big Picture (Match Outcome)

Predicting the fundamental story of the match?

Correct Match Winner: 25 points

Correct Number of Sets (e.g., predicting 3 sets when it was a 3-set match): 20 points

Your Score for Level 1:

You predicted Federer would win, and he did. +25 points.

You predicted a 2-set match, but it went to 3. +0 points.

Level 2: Set-by-Set Breakdown

Predicting the flow of the match.

Correct Winner of Each Set: 10 points per set

Correct Exact Score of Each Set (Bonus): 15 points per set

Your Score for Level 2:

Set 1: You predicted Federer, but Nadal won. +0 points.

Set 2: You predicted Federer, and he won. +10 points.

Set 3: You didn't predict a third set, so +0 points.

You didn't get any of the exact set scores right, so +0 bonus points.

Level 3: The Fine Details

This part acts as a great tie-breaker.

Correct Total Games Won by Match Winner: 10 points

Calculation: In reality, Federer won 4 + 6 + 6 = 16 games. You predicted he'd win 7 + 6 = 13. No match.

Correct Overall Game Difference: 10 points

Calculation: The actual game difference was 16 (Fed) - 11 (Nadal) = 5. You predicted a difference of 13 (Fed) - 9 (Nadal) = 4. Close, but not exact.

Your Score for Level 3:

You didn't predict the correct total games for the winner. +0 points.

You didn't predict the correct overall game difference. +0 points.

Final prediction score:

Level 1: 25 points

Level 2: 10 points

Level 3: 0 points

Total Score: 35 points

By using this you can achive who did better prediction,

World Cup teams who only draw in the group stage have only ever been second or third in the group.

In the history of the FIFA World Cup, a team drawing all of their matches in the group stage (if there was one) has happened nine times:

1958, Group 3: Wales drew 1-1 to both Hungary and Mexico, before 0-0 to Sweden. They won a playoff game against Hungary to be second in group.

1958, Group 4: England drew 2-2 to Soviet Union, 0-0 to Brazil, and 2-2 to Austria. They lost a playoff game against Soviet Union to be third in group.

1982, Group 1: Italy drew 0-0 to Poland, then 1-1 to both Peru and Cameroon. They had better goals-for to be second in group.

1982, Group 1: Cameroon drew 0-0 to both Peru and Poland, then 1-1 to Italy. They had worse goals-for to be third in group.

1990, Group F: Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with England, 0-0 with Egypt, and 1-1 with Netherlands. They were perfectly tied and split by drawing of lots to be second in group.

1990, Group F: Netherlands drew 1-1 with Egypt, 0-0 with England, and 1-1 with Republic of Ireland. They were perfectly tied and split by drawing of lots to be third in group. They still advanced as the third-in-group team with the third-best record.

1998, Group B: Chile drew 2-2 with Italy, then 1-1 with both Austria and Cameroon. They were second in group.

1998, Group E: Belgium drew 0-0 with Netherlands, 2-2 with Mexico, and 1-1 with South Korea. They were third in group.

2010, Group F: New Zealand drew 1-1 with both Slovakia and Italy, then drew 0-0 with Paraguay. They were third in group.

text:
The greatest supposed biological advantage in sport of having XY chromosomes is a high natural level of self-generated testosterone. I'm not sure your expectations are accurate as to the effect of this high level on doping test results. I make no presumption whether Khelif actually has that advantage.

In short: doping tests aren't what could rule out Khelif, or what ruled out Semenya, because the doping tests are specifically designed to ignore natural testosterone levels. Semenya was ruled out by a separate  (non-doping-related) limit on natural testosterone for middle-distance running. Khelif may or may not be ruled out by the genetic test due to be introduced for boxing.

The reason why Khelif (or anyone else) might have passed eligibility before, and not pass it in future, is simply that the rules and/or the application of those rules can change over time. The IOC has accused the IBA of being... inconsistent... in its past application of these and other rules, and it's unclear to me how the IBA came to pass Khelif and then later fail her. The IBA has opted not to reveal what tests they used, let alone the results. The criteria very specifically have been changed by World Boxing with their announced introduction of a genetic test.

In much longer form: Semenya didn't fail a doping test either. A rule was introduced by the IAAF in 2011-ish for a few athletics events, that excluded her and others with naturally high testosterone levels from those events. Prior to that rule change, she was qualified for the events. Even after the rule she was still qualified for other IAAF-administered events in which she had no desire to compete.

Externally-introduced/synthetic testosterone doping was banned by the IAAF long, long before that. Testosterone is absolute basic, route-1 doping. WADA routinely tested for it, Semenya always passed those tests. That doping test is not "you can't have more than this amount of testosterone", it's "you can't have evidence you're taking testosterone". So that rule caused Semenya no trouble. Because she wasn't doping.

AFAIK boxing (IBA, IOC or World Boxing) has introduced no rule on natural testosterone levels that's analogous to the rule that demanded Semenya would have to suppress testosterone to be eligible for middle-distance events. But if there is one, it's not relevant to Khelif, because even the IBA (which disqualified her) says that testosterone level was not the reason.

So, Khelif hasn't failed a testosterone test of any kind: either for natural levels or for doping. But then, we do not expect people to fail doping tests for having high natural testosterone levels. So this proves nothing one way or the other about whether she has a natural advantage, either due to chromosomes or any other reason.

Now you might ask: if the supposed advantage is naturally high testosterone, why not ban naturally high testosterone? This is what the IAAF did for women's middle-distance running in 2011.

The answer is that sport in general, and boxing in particular, doesn't ideally want to set a maximum testosterone level, and neither does it want to ban all competitors with natural advantages. Not that it's any of my business for any individual, but I do personally suspect that essentially all elite boxers, male and female, have higher-than-average natural testosterone to some extent. World Boxing obviously is not doing this to create opportunities for people of only average testosterone! There are loads of sports in which high natural testosterone is an advantage, just as there are loads of sports in which being tall is an advantage (to a point). This is why there are loads of elite competitors in all sports who have high testosterone and are tall. In boxing, weight is an advantage too, especially when that weight consists of muscle. But sports don't want "low testosterone" or "short" categories: they want "women's" categories (and, in boxing, they do want weight categories but not, for example, reach categories). So, that's what sports authorities are still trying to figure out - how to define eligibility for women's categories in sport. There are various possibilities: "the gender you identify as"; "the gender on your passport"; "the gender you were assigned at birth"; and "whether your 23rd chromosomes are XX, XY, or something else" can all potentially differ. So whichever they pick creates a slightly different category, but any of those is closer to defining gender or sex as it's commonly understood, than "your testosterone level". Even though the latter is probably more relevant to the actual boxing.

Move forwards quickly to meet the rolling ball

Bend your knees to kneel with one knee on the floor

Receive the ball and return over/under arm, depending on the situation

When you don't know the speed of the ball or there is uneven bounce.

text:
Why isn’t a 30-30 tie also called “DEUCE”, the same as a 40-40 tie?

Here's the difference why ONLY a 40-40 tie should be called --"DEUCE"

It's true that when the score is tied at 30-30 or 40-40, going forward the first player to get TWO consecutive points will win the game. So why not call it "DEUCE" in both cases -- both when it's tied at 30-30 and when it's tied at 40-40? What's the difference?

Here's the difference?

In tennis, to win a game, you need to win a MINIMUM of 4 points.

When the game is tied at 30-30, each player has won 2 points each. If one of the players goes on to win the next two points, that player wins the game and that player would have won the game by winning a total of 4 points, the MINIMUM number of points needed to win a game.

But when the game is tied at 40-40, each player has won 3 points each. The player that goes on to win will need to win two consecutive points to win the game. That player will need at least 5 points to win the game. In other words, when the score is tied at 40-40, the winning player will need to win MORE THAN the MINIMUM 4 points to win the game.

So, calling a 40-40 tie, "DEUCE", means not only that one of the players needs to win TWO consecutive points to win the game, but the player ALSO needs to win MORE THAN the MINIMUM 4 points to win the game, which isn't the case with a 30-30 tie. It is what differentiates one from the other.

Accordingly, the usage of the word, "DEUCE, should be reserved for a 40-40 tie ONLY, to denote a tie that requires the winning player to win MORE THAN the MINIMUM 4 points to win the game.

Everton finished 5 points above the relegation zone in 1913/14, then won the title in 1914/15.

Leicester remain the first and only team to achieve it in the postwar era.

The cricket long barrier technique

The long barrier is the safest technique to control a cricket ball that is travelling along the ground.

Move towards the ball at a controlled speed.

Get in line with the ball and get your whole body behind the ball.

As quickly as possible bend both knees and twist sideways so that the knee of your strong leg touches the ground and touches the back of the heel of the other leg.

Extend arms downwards, spread hands wide with little fingers touching each other.

Pick up the ball and draw into the body, then stand up ready to make the best decision.

Nij addressed issues of "fairness" (https://sports.stackexchange.com/a/29876/13730). However, I think history is a more likely explanation of why a kick after safety is different from a kick after a touchdown or field goal.

Dig into the history of American Football and you'll find that what is now called a safety was essentially the same as a touchback. (Football Archaeology (https://www.footballarchaeology.com/p/a-word-on-football-rouge-safety-and) was the first web site I found documenting this, although I remember reading about it in a forgotten book decades ago.) In fact, a team could start a play from scrimmage outside its own endzone, run backwards into its own endzone, take a knee, and then start with a new set of downs at their 25 yard line. They were said to be doing this "for safety". Obviously such a rule could be - and was - abused. Thus the rule was changed so that the team with the ball couldn't do this intentionally, and doing so would result in a kick from the 25. Given the linkage between the safety and the touchback, it would make sense that moving the starting point after a touchback to the 20 yard line would also move the kicking point after a safety.

Under the current playoff rules, this is 15-2, and here's how. Let's use the AFC for this example and assume games haven't been played in 2024.

You need two teams from each division. You also need to minimize interaction between teams competing for this. To do so, you need to use previous year rankings. For this example, we will use the Chiefs and Broncos (2023 West #1 and West #3 respectively) to determine teams.

We do not want to play other #1 and #3 seeds competing for this in out-of-rotation games based on the previous season, and therefore we need to play them as part of the 3-year conference rotation. Therefore, the Ravens and Steelers (2023 North #1 and North #3) are also competing for this. Next, since we can not have other #1 and #3 seeds face off against these teams, that leaves us with the #2 and #4 seeds from the previous season, though the West and North have fulfilled their two team quota. Therefore, welcome in the Dolphins, Patriots, Jaguars, and Titans.

Now that we have our eight teams, we need to minimize losses, and to do that we need to calculate how many games these teams will see another team competing for the honor. Let's use the Chiefs. They have two games against the Chargers, not ideal but everyone has two games against their divisional opponents. They also face the AFC North for their three year rotation, so the Chiefs face the Ravens and Steelers. However, seeing that the previous #2 and #4 seeds are not their division's #1 from the previous season, the Chiefs won't face any of them. This works out the same with all other teams, meaning that each team only faces someone fighting for the ultimate tiebreaker four times.

Using this revelation, we can use the concept of splitting games. Intra-division, each team fighting can get a split with their divisional rival, giving all eight one loss. From there, the two rotational conference games can be split, giving everyone a total of two losses. Assuming that all eight teams win every other game they play, all eight would end up with a 15-2 record. In this case, someone goes home, and it's probably gonna be on a fairly awful tiebreaker.

For those of you who don't know what redshirting is, it is defined as:

Redshirt, in United States college athletics, is a delay or suspension of an athlete's participation in order to lengthen their period of eligibility.

I'm going to assume that this question asks about GPA, as that just makes the most sense. In that case, yes, there is a cutoff, and that is 2.3, according to this (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redshirt_(college_sports)#:%7E:text=Under%20these%20new%20requirements%2C%20a%20student%20athlete%20who,the%20team%2C%20but%20may%20not%20participate%20in%20competition.) wikipedia article.

In 2016, a new status could be applied to prospective student athletes, dubbed an academic redshirt. That year, the NCAA started enforcing new, stricter admissions requirements for incoming athletic freshmen. Under these new requirements, a student athlete who meets a school's own academic admission requirements but does not meet the NCAA requirement of a 2.3 GPA across four years, may enter school as an academic redshirt. This student can receive an athletic scholarship and practice with the team, but may not participate in competition.

(Bolding mine)

In terms of a time cutoff, generally, there isn’t a specific deadline to be redshirted.

text:
Because there are runners on 2nd and 3rd, it is not a force out to tag out R2. So, all that matters is whether or not R3 scores before or after the tag. If R3 scores prior to the tag, the run counts. Otherwise, the 3rd out has been recorded, and the run would not count.

This is not the case if the 3rd out is a force out. So, suppose that it's bases loaded, and R2 is tagged out. In that case, that out is a force out, and regardless of whether or not R3 scores prior to the out, the run would not count.

From the MLB rulebook (https://content.mlb.com/documents/2/2/4/305750224/2019_Official_Baseball_Rules_FINAL_.pdf), Rule 5.08(a) details the requirements for scoring a run.

One run shall be scored each time a runner legally advances to and touches first, second, third and home base before three men are put out to end the inning.
EXCEPTION: A run is not scored if the runner advances to home base during a play in which the third out is made (1) by the batter-runner before he touches first base; (2) by any runner being forced out; or (3) by a preceding runner who is declared out because he failed to touch one of the bases.

At no level of baseball can a runner be put out by being contacted with a ball thrown by the defense (whether intentional or not).   The defense must make a proper tag, or on a force play, tag the base.

For MLB rules (https://mktg.mlbstatic.com/mlb/official-information/2024-official-baseball-rules.pdf), this is covered by 5.09(b).   The actions described do not meet any of the situations under this rule, especially not 5.09(b)(4), which is being tagged while off a base.

A TAG is the action of a fielder in touching a base with his body
while holding the ball securely and firmly in his hand or glove; or
touching a runner with the ball, or with his hand or glove holding the
ball (not including hanging laces alone), while holding the ball
securely and firmly in his hand or glove. [...]

Since the ball struck you in the back while running, it seems unlikely that anyone would suggest that this was intentional interference on your part.   But in a case where someone moves at the last second and is struck, they could be called out under 5.09(b)(3) for intentional interference with a thrown ball.

It is possible for a member of the defense to pick up the deflected ball and complete the tag properly if you have still not yet reached the base.

is it an error on the SS?

Maybe.   If the scorer believes that the out would have been made with a reasonable throw, then an error would be appropriate.

text: The traditional definition of "Left On Base" is the number of players left on the field at the end of the inning. The individual statistic is absurd in my opinion. Two examples. Batter leads off the inning with a double. The next three batters strike out. Using individual left on base criteria there would be 3 players left on base, as each batter that struck out would be credited with a LOB. In reality, only 1 player was LOB. This stat is very useful for handicappers because it reflects "timely" hitting. Your best baseball teams always hit with men on base.
